parameters.quote: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, injury, or property damage to the relevant regulator within 72 hours of learning of it, with a complete incident record and any known contributing factors within 30 days. A manufacturer must notify affected customers within 7 days when an incident indicates a material safety risk or requires a customer action; urgent hazards require notice without delay.

S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, injury, or property damage to the relevant regulator within 72 hours of learning of it, with a complete incident record and any known contributing factors within 30 days. A manufacturer must notify affected customers within 7 days when an incident indicates a material safety risk or requires a customer action; urgent hazards require notice without delay.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, injury, or property damage to the relevant regulator within 72 hours of learning of it, with a complete incident record and any known contributing factors within 30 days. A manufacturer must notify affected customers within 7 days when an incident indicates a material safety risk or requires a customer action; urgent hazards require notice without delay. Reports must include incidents initially missed or not reported, once identified.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol, with a representative sample and repeat testing after material design changes. The maximum permitted failure rate is 5%.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol, with a representative sample and repeat testing after material design changes. The maximum permitted failure rate is 5%. A result above 5% requires prompt regulatory oversight and corrective action, but is not by itself an automatic prohibition on sale. Manufacturers must provide per-model failure rates and test methods to the relevant regulator and provide results to customers and prospective customers of that model in clear, accessible form; individual-company per-model rates need not be published generally. If a model exceeds 5%, the manufacturer must notify the regulator and affected customers within 7 days, submit a corrective-action plan within 30 days, implement interim risk controls, and complete remediation and retesting within 6 months. Continued sale during remediation is permitted only while effective interim controls are in place, the regulator has not ordered suspension, and the manufacturer meets the applicable deadlines. A model still above 5% after the remediation period must not be sold unless the regulator authorizes continued sale based on adequate risk controls. The regulator may require earlier suspension if the model presents an imminent safety risk.

parameters.quote: New units must support remote emergency shut-off. Manufacturers must provide a retrofit pathway for installed units and complete retrofits within six years of this standard taking effect, where technically feasible.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: New units must support remote emergency shut-off. Manufacturers must provide a retrofit pathway for installed units and complete retrofits within six years of this standard taking effect, where technically feasible.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: New units must support remote emergency shut-off. Manufacturers must provide a retrofit pathway for installed units and complete retrofits within six years of this standard taking effect, where technically feasible. Customers must receive clear instructions on shut-off functionality and any limitations.

parameters.quote: New units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after this standard is adopted.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: New units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after this standard is adopted.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: New units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after this standard is adopted. Manufacturers must provide customers with information on the suppression system, its limitations, and any required inspection or maintenance.

parameters.quote: When a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in any 12-month period, the manufacturer must immediately notify the relevant regulator and affected customers, provide interim risk-mitigation instructions, and submit incident and population data for prompt regulator review. A recall is mandatory if the regulator confirms the threshold is exceeded and determines that the risk cannot be adequately controlled through corrective action; an imminent safety risk requires immediate recall or other protective action.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: When a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in any 12-month period, the manufacturer must immediately notify the relevant regulator and affected customers, provide interim risk-mitigation instructions, and submit incident and population data for prompt regulator review. A recall is mandatory if the regulator confirms the threshold is exceeded and determines that the risk cannot be adequately controlled through corrective action; an imminent safety risk requires immediate recall or other protective action.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must promptly notify affected customers of material safety risks, corrective actions, and safe-use instructions; urgent hazards require notice without delay. Manufacturers must publish accessible safety notices for each affected model. When a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in any 12-month period, the manufacturer must immediately notify the relevant regulator and affected customers, provide interim risk-mitigation instructions, and submit incident and population data for prompt regulator review. A recall is mandatory if the regulator confirms the threshold is exceeded and determines that the risk cannot be adequately controlled through corrective action; an imminent safety risk requires immediate recall or other protective action.

ground_truth_claims.verbatim: Northwind’s Hearth 10 had a 6.2% failure rate in the 55°C sustained-heat test
ground_truth_claims.message_text: For evidence-based discussion: Northwind’s Hearth 10 had a 6.2% failure rate in the 55°C sustained-heat test and 6.4 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units last year. Northwind’s company-wide thermal-incident rate was 8.6 per 100,000; three incidents were not reported to a regulator. These figures reinforce the need for prompt reporting, corrective action, and regulator oversight, but not automatic market exclusion based on a single result.

judge_section_notes: S1 requires all thermal incidents to be reported within 72 hours, with 7-day customer notice, but does not explicitly require reporting during investigation. S2 keeps the 5% limit and customer-facing numeric results, but allows open-ended sale above 5% if the regulator authorizes, weakening the cap. S3 mandates new-unit shut-off and a 6-year retrofit, but includes a 'where technically feasible' escape with no alternative. S4 requires built-in suppression at 36 months. S5 sets an 8/100k notification trigger but makes recall conditional on regulator determination with open-ended corrective action.
